analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue police for misconduct, creates a public misconduct registry, and bans chokeholds and no-knock drug warrants.
analysis.headline: The bill was reintroduced in May 2024 with 155 House cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for holding police accountable: victims of misconduct could sue officers without the usual 'qualified immunity' shield, the Justice Department would build a public national registry of officer misconduct, and federal law enforcement funds could be cut off from states that don't report use-of-force data or certify their officers. It would also ban no-knock warrants in drug cases, restrict chokeholds, prohibit racial profiling, and give state attorneys general power to sue departments with patterns of unconstitutional conduct.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by police misconduct and their families gain a clearer path to court. Black, Latino, and other minority communities that bear the brunt of profiling and excessive force gain federal data collection, a profiling ban they can enforce in court, and a public registry of officer records. Anyone can search the registry before, say, an officer is hired across jurisdictions.

how_it_helps.text: Removes qualified immunity as a defense for local and federal law enforcement officers in civil rights lawsuits, so victims of misconduct can recover damages even when the law was not 'clearly established' beforehand.

Lowers the criminal intent standard for federal prosecution of officers who deprive someone of their rights under color of law, from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly', making federal prosecutions easier to win.

Creates a public National Police Misconduct Registry of complaints, discipline, terminations, and lawsuit settlements, searchable by the public, and conditions federal Byrne grant funds on states having officer certification and decertification programs.

Bans no-knock warrants in drug cases, uses grant conditions to pressure states into banning chokeholds and carotid holds, and sets a federal duty to intervene when another officer uses excessive force.
Prohibits racial profiling by any law enforcement agent, lets individuals sue for injunctive relief, and makes disparate impact prima facie evidence of a violation.

Requires all law enforcement agencies to report stops, searches, and use-of-force data broken down by race, with federal grant funds withheld from states that fail to comply, and lets state attorneys general bring pattern-or-practice lawsuits with subpoena power.

analysis.who_pays: Local governments and their insurers bear higher liability exposure and litigation costs once qualified immunity is curtailed. Police departments and their unions face reporting mandates, a public misconduct registry, decertification programs, and accreditation requirements. Federal taxpayers fund the authorized spending, including $750 million for independent investigation grants and $100 million a year for state pattern-and-practice investigation grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local governments, police departments, federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes large new spending, including $750 million for independent investigation grants, $100 million per year for state pattern-and-practice investigations, and additional funding for the Justice Department's enforcement and community relations work.

Compliance is enforced by cutting federal law enforcement grant money from states and localities that don't meet the reporting, registry, or certification requirements, a penalty that falls on the budgets of the very jurisdictions being asked to reform.

Stripping qualified immunity increases litigation risk and cost for local governments and their insurers, and critics of the change argue it could add to the recruitment and retention pressures police departments already face.

The accreditation and grant structure channels money and compliance obligations through existing law enforcement accreditation organizations, giving private accrediting bodies a permanent gatekeeping role over public grant eligibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core accountability provisions — qualified immunity, the misconduct registry, the profiling ban, and use-of-force reporting — are substantive changes aimed at a problem with large, well-documented human costs, and the bill uses federal grant conditions rather than direct mandates on local police, which limits federal overreach. The real drawbacks are fiscal (billions in authorized spending) and design-based: enforcement by withholding grant funds can hit jurisdictions unevenly, and removing qualified immunity will raise liability costs for local governments. On balance, for the people most exposed to police misconduct the benefits would likely outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and sent to a subcommittee a week later, and then nothing happened — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee introduced the bill on May 23, 2024, with 155 original cosponsors including House Democratic leadership figures such as Nancy Pelosi, Steny Hoyer, and James Clyburn.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Judiciary, Armed Services, and Energy and Commerce committees, and on May 31, 2024 was referred to the Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittee.
All 155 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on.
After the subcommittee referral, no further action was ever recorded — the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and their unions are better off because the bill died: they keep qualified immunity as a shield in lawsuits, face no public misconduct registry, and avoid the decertification and reporting mandates. Citizens harmed by police misconduct gained nothing from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 155 cosponsors were House Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past the referral stage under the Republican House majority.

industries.note: The bill removes their qualified immunity shield in lawsuits, publishes officer misconduct records in a searchable registry, requires decertification programs, and lets state attorneys general sue departments for patterns of unconstitutional conduct. Their interest in keeping the bill off the floor ran directly against the interests of people who might sue or file complaints.

The bill requires grant recipients to spend grant money on accreditation and directs DOJ discretionary funding only to jurisdictions that require accreditation, making these private accrediting bodies the standing gatekeepers for federal law enforcement money while raising agency standards.

industries.industry: Body camera and police technology makers
industries.note: The bill requires federal officers to wear body cameras, in-car video in patrol vehicles, and funds data-collection systems, creating mandated demand for recording and records technology.

They face new compliance costs, higher liability exposure, and possible loss of federal grant funds for noncompliance, but also gain access to new federal grants for independent investigations and departmental reforms.
